Which choke for which distance

Distance to the target is the main factor in choosing a choke. The two disciplines set their distances in different ways.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Targets imitate hunting shots, so they are set at distances where a hunter could cleanly shoot a bird. They are not so close that the meat would be ruined, and not so far that the bird would only be wounded. The rules call this hunting ethics.

Compak® Sporting

Targets fly over a marked rectangle 35–40 m wide and 25 m deep in front of the shooting positions.

  1. Up to about 20 m: cylinder or a very light choke (1/8).
  2. About 20–30 m: improved cylinder (1/4) or light modified.
  3. About 30–35 m: modified (1/2).
  4. Beyond about 35 m: improved modified (3/4), and occasionally full.

This is a rough guide that many coaches use for lead shot No. 7½–9. It is not a rule: coaches and experienced shooters have their own preferences.

Tip: Judging distance is hard for a beginner. Look at where you are likely to shoot the target, not where it comes from. Ask your coach or an experienced shooter in your squad: on a shooting ground that is an ordinary question.

The type of target matters too. A mini is small, so it needs a denser pattern. A battue is a thin, flat target that often flies edge-on, so you see only its thin side. It is easier to break when it turns and shows its flat face. A rabbit rolls along the ground and is tougher than a standard target.

In an over-and-under the more open choke usually goes in the barrel that fires first, and the tighter one in the second. A 1/4 and 1/2 pair (IC and M) is a popular all-round choice for many Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ stands and for a whole Compak® Sporting round, where chokes may not be changed.

Tip: Advice for beginners: do not overdo tight chokes. On the close and medium targets that beginners shoot most, a more open choke forgives small pointing errors and builds confidence. Once your technique is more consistent, you can experiment.

Key points

  • Choose the choke for the distance at which you will shoot.
  • A rough guide: up to 20 m cylinder or 1/8, 20–30 m IC or LM, 30–35 m M, beyond 35 m IM.
  • More open choke for the first shot, tighter for the second.
  • An IC and M pair is a popular all-round choice.
  • Beginners usually do better with more open chokes on close and medium targets.

Did you know?

Many experienced Sporting™ shooters use fairly open chokes even for far targets. They rely on precise pointing rather than on a tight pattern.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Which choke roughly suits a target at about 30–35 m?

    1. Cylinder
    2. Improved cylinder (1/4)
    3. Modified (1/2)
    4. Extra full
    Answer

    Modified (1/2)

    At 30–35 m modified is the usual choice, but this is only a guide.

  2. Which barrel of an over-and-under usually gets the more open choke?

    1. The one that fires first
    2. The one that fires second
    3. The same one in both barrels
    4. The rules do not allow it
    Answer

    The one that fires first

    The first shot is usually the closer one, so the first barrel gets the more open choke.

  3. Why are beginners advised not to overdo tight chokes?

    1. Tight chokes are banned for beginners
    2. A narrow pattern forgives fewer errors
    3. They make the recoil much harder
    4. They wear out the barrel faster
    Answer

    A narrow pattern forgives fewer errors

    A narrow pattern needs precise pointing; on close and medium targets a more open choke forgives more.
